Newborn guinea pigs, known as pups, enter the world remarkably precocial, with their eyes open and a full coat of fur. The average wet weight at birth for a pup is 85 grams [Wwb = 85 grams], a substantial mass that reflects the species' extended gestation period relative to other rodents. This considerable birth weight is made possible by a gestation period of 68 days [tg = 68 days], a duration more typical of ungulates than small mammals, which is sustained at the species' normal body temperature of 39 °C [T = 39 °C]. The pups' advanced state of development at birth is a clear adaptation to a terrestrial lifestyle, allowing them to thermoregulate and follow their mother shortly after parturition. This initial investment in neonatal mass is a cornerstone of the life-history strategy of Cavia porcellus, allowing for a relatively rapid transition to independent feeding.

The period following parturition is marked by intensive maternal care, centered around lactation. Pups are weaned after a relatively short suckling period, specifically 18 days [tx = 18 days] at a typical core body temperature of 39 °C [T = 39 °C]. At the point of nutritional independence, a weanling pup will have grown substantially, achieving a wet weight of 228 grams [Wwx = 228 grams]. This rapid growth rate from a 85-gram (85 grams) [Wwb = 85 grams] neonate to a 228-gram weanling is fueled entirely by the mother's milk, a highly nutritious food source. The transition to a solid food diet occurs quickly, as the young are already nibbling on hay and pellets alongside the adults within the first few days of life, though milk remains the primary energy source until the official cessation of lactation at 18 days.

Sexual maturation in the guinea pig is a sexually dimorphic process, with females reaching puberty earlier than males. Under the standard physiological temperature of 39 °C [T = 39 °C], females attain sexual maturity at 66 days since birth [tp = 66 days since birth]. In contrast, males require a longer developmental period, with the time since birth at puberty being 76 days [tp = 76 days] at the same temperature of 39 °C [T = 39 °C]. This divergence in maturation timelines is common in polygynous or promiscuous mating systems, where female reproductive development is prioritized, and males benefit from a slightly longer juvenile phase to compete effectively for mating opportunities. The onset of puberty marks the transition from an immature individual to a reproductively viable adult.

Adulthood in Cavia porcellus is characterized by rapid and efficient reproduction. Females exhibit a maximum reproductive rate derived from 3.8 pups per litter [N_R_i = 3.8 pups per litter], combined with a high breeding frequency of roughly 5 litters annually [F_R_i = roughly 5 litters annually]. This remarkable fecundity is sustained at the species' stable core temperature of 39 °C [T = 39 °C], which supports the high metabolic costs of gestation and lactation. The short gestation of 68 days allows females to be pregnant nearly back-to-back, as they can enter postpartum estrus just hours after giving birth. This strategy of a moderately large litter size coupled with a high frequency of litters allows a single female to produce upward of 19 offspring per year, a key reason for the species' success as both a laboratory model and a domesticated animal.

The lifespan of the guinea pig is notable for its length when compared to other rodents of similar body mass. Under captive conditions maintained at 39 °C [T = 39 °C], the maximum recorded longevity is 12 years [am = 12 years]. This extended lifespan, equivalent to approximately 4,380 days, is accompanied by a long period of reproductive viability. While females reach puberty early, the ultimate adult wet weight for a well-fed individual can reach up to 728 grams [Wwi = up to 728 grams]. This relatively slow pace of life for a rodent, characterized by a long gestation, a long lifespan, and a high neonatal investment, aligns with a "slow" life-history strategy more common in larger mammals, yet the guinea pig achieves this within a small-bodied framework.
